 Stethoscope blues 
 Stethoscope blues 
 Anil Abraham / Nov 10, 2026, 07:50 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print Photo credit: AP Tomato Thimappa walked into the clinic, looking very excited. “Have you heard about this Temple thing?” he asked me enthusiastically. His was the classic case of the patient who always felt he knew more than the doctor. Based on extensive study, by scrolling social media, he was well-informed about the latest in medical marvels, miracles, and magic remedies. I held back from commenting. Because the term temple did ring a bell, but I wanted to make sure we were discussing the same controversy. “It’s a device doc!” he announced. I have always been of the opinion that our body is a temple, and is best left to its own devices. But he let out a whoop of joy and continued his Oura-farming. Doctors treating illness is not fashionable anymore, apparently. Wellness devices are the latest trend, and at a cost of tens of thousands, they are a steal. Wearable fitness trackers can tell you about the steps you take, and the steps you need to take to remain healthy. They can monitor your blood pressure and brain flow, while gently suggesting dos and don’ts, to prevent dementia, diabetes, and diarrhea. I have my own unbearable fitness tracker at home – Kamala gives me advice non-stop and completely free. Throughout Diwali she kept making ominous sounds, whenever I glanced sideways at a kaju katli . But this new device, Thimappa told me, could be pasted on the temple, and would temporarily predict one’s deepest desires, through the pulsations of the superficial temporal artery. Empathy was being replaced with entropy. Before I was completely bheja fried, I tried explaining the deeper concepts of cerebral blood flow. But Thimappa was convinced that this was a no-brainer, and undeniable proof that India has survived the brain drain. I offered the concept of evidence-based medicine, but he was a fervent fan of eloquence-based medicine. Since we had discovered Zero, he felt there was zero need for tangible scientific proof. Even if the brain doctor or the liver doctor and other dear concerned Indian doctors, were raising an objection, his faith in the fallible was firmer than ever. Thimappa wanted me to keep an open mind about tech in medicine – whether it was a device or just devious. But as Richard Dawkins once said, “By all means let’s be open-minded, but not so open-minded that our brains drop out.”
